paragraphs.title: The Lament over Pharaoh and the Humiliation of Egypt

answers: Pharaoh king of Egypt
The king of Babylon
The king of Edom
easy.explanation: The Lord told Ezekiel to take up a lamentation for Pharaoh king of Egypt.
easy.q: For whom was Ezekiel told to take up a lamentation?

answers: A young lion
A whale
An eagle
easy.explanation: Pharaoh is compared to a whale in the seas, coming forth with his rivers.
easy.q: To what is Pharaoh compared in the seas?

answers: A net
A wall
A crown
easy.explanation: The Lord said, “I will therefore spread out my net over thee.”
easy.q: What would the Lord spread over Pharaoh?

answers: He would be left upon the land
He would be returned to the rivers
He would be made king over many nations
medium.explanation: The Lord said He would leave Pharaoh upon the land and cast him forth upon the open field.
medium.q: What would happen to Pharaoh after he was caught?

answers: The nations would honor it
The fowls and beasts would feed upon it
It would be buried in a royal tomb
medium.explanation: The fowls of heaven and beasts of the earth would remain upon and be filled with Pharaoh.
medium.q: What would happen to Pharaoh’s body on the land?

answers: Pharaoh calmed the rivers
Pharaoh disturbed and fouled the waters
Pharaoh dried up the rivers
medium.explanation: The image describes Pharaoh as disturbing the waters and fouling the rivers.
medium.q: What does “troubledst the waters with thy feet” mean in context?

answers: He appears powerful, yet he is captured and humiliated
He appears weak, yet he conquers every nation
He appears righteous, yet he becomes a priest
challenge.explanation: Pharaoh is pictured as a mighty creature, but the Lord captures him and casts him onto the land.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in the description of Pharaoh?

answers: He voluntarily gives up his kingdom
His harmful power results in his capture and destruction
He gives his rivers to another king
challenge.explanation: Pharaoh’s proud and destructive conduct is followed by the Lord’s judgment and his capture.
challenge.q: How does Pharaoh’s pride lead to his downfall?

answers: They praise Pharaoh
They rescue Egypt
They help capture and humiliate Pharaoh
challenge.explanation: The Lord’s net is spread with a company of many people, who bring Pharaoh up in the net.
challenge.q: What role do the many people have in the prophecy?

paragraphs.title: Destruction as a Cosmic Event and the Shock of the Nations

answers: They would be covered and darkened
They would be filled with rainbows
They would become brighter
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would cover the heaven and make its stars dark.
easy.q: What would happen to the heavens when Egypt fell?

answers: The sun and the moon
The fire and the lightning
The stars only
easy.explanation: The sun would be covered with a cloud, and the moon would not give her light.
easy.q: Which heavenly lights are specifically mentioned?

answers: With celebration
With indifference
With amazement and fear
easy.explanation: Many people would be amazed, and their kings would be horribly afraid.
easy.q: How would the nations respond to Egypt’s destruction?

answers: It presents the destruction as a vast, world-shaking event
It explains how stars are created
It hides Pharaoh’s victory
medium.explanation: The darkened heavens portray Egypt’s fall as greater than an ordinary political defeat.
medium.q: What does the darkening of the heavenly lights communicate about Egypt’s fall?

answers: Because of a shortage of water
Because the sword would be brandished before them
Because Pharaoh would return to power
medium.explanation: The nations would fear when the Lord’s sword was brandished before them.
medium.q: Why would the kings and peoples tremble?

answers: To make them shine more brightly
To darken the heavenly lights
To bring the stars nearer to earth
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the Lord’s judgment as a darkening of the stars and other lights.
medium.q: What does “make the stars thereof dark” mean in context?

answers: To present the fall as an event of enormous significance
To describe the beginning of the stars
To portray Egyptians traveling through heaven
challenge.explanation: The darkened sun, moon, and stars give Egypt’s downfall universal and dramatic significance.
challenge.q: Why is cosmic imagery used in the prophecy against Egypt?

answers: The nations rejoice, and Egypt becomes stronger
Egypt is destroyed, and the nations and kings are terrified
The heavens brighten, and Pharaoh rescues the nations
challenge.explanation: Egypt’s destruction is followed by amazement, fear, and trembling among the nations.
challenge.q: What sequence is described in these verses?

answers: The judgment is seen as a threat to powerful rulers generally
Only common people are affected
The kings have never heard of Egypt
challenge.explanation: The fear of kings shows that Egypt’s fall affects and alarms those who possess power.
challenge.q: What can be inferred because even kings are afraid?

paragraphs.title: The Sword of the King of Babylon and the Desolation of Egypt

answers: The king of Babylon’s
The king of Edom’s
The king of Assyria’s
easy.explanation: The Lord declares, “The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon thee.”
easy.q: Whose sword would come upon Egypt?

answers: Only the rivers
The multitude and the beasts
Only Pharaoh’s palace
easy.explanation: The multitude of Egypt would fall, and all its beasts would also be destroyed.
easy.q: What would be destroyed in Egypt?

answers: The daughters of the nations
Only Babylonian soldiers
Only Pharaoh’s family
easy.explanation: The daughters of the nations would lament for Egypt and all her multitude.

answers: They would disappear completely
They would become like oil
They would remain disturbed and muddy
medium.explanation: The Lord said He would make the waters deep and cause the rivers to run like oil.
medium.q: What would happen to Egypt’s waters after its people and beasts were gone?

answers: There would be no more people or beasts to tread in them
The beasts would drink all the rivers
People would build dams across them
medium.explanation: The foot of man and the hoofs of beasts would no longer trouble the waters.
medium.q: Why would the waters no longer be troubled?

answers: They would build cities for Egypt
They would mourn for Egypt
They would fight beside Egypt
medium.explanation: To lament means to mourn or express sorrow over Egypt’s destruction.
medium.q: What does “the daughters of the nations shall lament her” mean?

answers: A land full of life becomes desolate and empty
A barren land becomes wealthy
A mountain land becomes snowy
challenge.explanation: The land that was full of people and beasts becomes desolate after its inhabitants are struck.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between Egypt’s former condition and its condition after judgment?

answers: Egypt’s desolation is visible and grievous to all
They want to restore Pharaoh’s throne
They depend on Egypt’s rivers for food
challenge.explanation: The widespread destruction of Egypt calls forth mourning from the nations.
challenge.q: Why is the lament of the daughters of the nations fitting?

answers: It will come through military power
It will happen only through drought
It will happen by Egypt’s choice
challenge.explanation: The passage directly identifies the sword of Babylon and the swords of the mighty as the means of Egypt’s fall.
challenge.q: What does the mention of Babylon’s sword reveal about Egypt’s downfall?

paragraphs.title: The Descent of the Nations to the Netherworld

answers: Into the nether parts of the earth
To the tops of the mountains
Into the rivers of Egypt
easy.explanation: They are cast down to the nether parts of the earth with those who go down into the pit.
easy.q: Where is Ezekiel told to cast down Egypt and the famous nations?

answers: Asshur
Israel
Moab
easy.explanation: Asshur is specifically mentioned among the fallen nations.
easy.q: Which kingdom is named among those in the pit?

answers: As rulers still commanding nations
As slain and fallen by the sword
As builders of new cities
easy.explanation: The nations are described as uncircumcised and slain by the sword.
easy.q: How are the kingdoms described in the netherworld?

answers: They are fallen powers lying among the dead
They help Pharaoh win a battle
They remain in the land of the living
medium.explanation: Each is described as a once-feared power that has fallen and lies in the pit.
medium.q: What do Asshur, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal have in common?

answers: Their strength did not prevent their downfall
They had no rivers
They refused to bury Pharaoh
medium.explanation: Although they caused terror in the land of the living, they now bear shame among the slain.
medium.q: Why is the shame of the nations emphasized?

answers: Those who descend to the place of the dead
Those who go down to draw water
Those who descend from the mountains to trade
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the dead who descend into the pit or netherworld.
medium.q: What does “them that go down into the pit” mean in this lament?

answers: They go from terrifying the living to lying powerless in the pit
They go from weakness to greater kingship
They go from wandering to living in palaces
challenge.explanation: The nations that once caused terror are now slain, powerless, and ashamed.
challenge.q: What change in the nations’ status is emphasized?

answers: To show that they kept their symbols of power but were not saved by them
To show that they are still victorious
To describe how they built their graves
challenge.explanation: The mighty went down with their weapons, yet their weapons could not prevent their judgment.
challenge.q: Why are weapons mentioned beside the fallen warriors?

answers: The many nations fell and share the same fate
Every nation received a new kingdom
The passage describes a journey between cities
challenge.explanation: The graves surrounding the various peoples stress the widespread and shared nature of their defeat.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the repeated mention of graves around the nations?

paragraphs.title: Pharaoh Joins the Slain of the Sword

answers: With those slain by the sword
With the priests
With the living kings of Babylon
easy.explanation: Pharaoh would lie with the uncircumcised and with those slain with the sword.

answers: Edom, the princes of the north, and the Zidonians
Israel, Judah, and Moab
Babylon, Media, and Persia
easy.explanation: The passage names Edom, the princes of the north, and the Zidonians.
easy.q: Which peoples are mentioned among those joining Pharaoh in the pit?

answers: The slain nations and all his multitude
The victory of his army
The restoration of Egypt’s rivers
easy.explanation: Pharaoh would see the slain nations and his own multitude slain by the sword.
easy.q: What would Pharaoh see in the netherworld?

answers: An honorable burial and the status of a victorious ruler
The ability to speak with other nations
The ability to see the rivers
medium.explanation: Pharaoh is placed among the uncircumcised and slain rather than receiving an honorable royal burial.
medium.q: What honor is denied to Pharaoh in this lament?

answers: They lie with the slain and bear shame
They rule in the land of the living
They rescue Egypt from destruction
medium.explanation: All are described as fallen and lying among those who went down to the pit.
medium.q: What do Pharaoh, Edom, and the Zidonians have in common?

answers: Fear and dread
Joy and celebration
Wisdom and instruction
medium.explanation: Terror means fear or dread; the Lord declares that His terror has been established in the land of the living.
medium.q: What does “terror” mean in “I have caused my terror in the land of the living”?

answers: Pharaoh’s terror is replaced by the Lord’s terror
Pharaoh becomes more frightening after death
The nations cease to fear every power
challenge.explanation: The final verses emphasize that the Lord has caused His terror in the land of the living while Pharaoh lies among the slain.
challenge.q: What is the central change concerning Pharaoh’s former terror?

answers: His fall is part of the shared fate of fallen powers
All the nations remained loyal to him
Egypt conquered all the nations
challenge.explanation: Pharaoh joins a company of rulers and nations that have fallen and gone down to the pit.
challenge.q: What does the joining of many nations to Pharaoh communicate?

answers: Pharaoh’s earthly terror ends, and the Lord’s authority is established
Pharaoh returns to rule after death
The nations restore Egypt’s honor
challenge.explanation: The conclusion places Pharaoh among the slain and declares that the Lord’s terror, not Pharaoh’s, prevails.
challenge.q: What idea summarizes the closing verses?
